claim: An imaging-based confined migration device with a stiffness gradient was developed.
source: Here, we develop an imaging-based confined migration device with a stiffness gradient.
evidence: The manuscript describes the development of this device in the methods and results sections, with experimental data showing its use.

claim: Amoeboid cells (T cells and neutrophils) can undergo durotaxis.
source: By tracking live cell trajectory and analyzing the directionality of T cells and neutrophils, we observe that amoeboid cells can durotax.
evidence: Supported by experimental tracking data, FMI measurements, and trajectory analysis shown in Figure 1.

claim: Amoeboid durotaxis involves non-muscle myosin IIA (NMIIA) polarization towards the soft-matrix-side.
source: We further delineate the underlying mechanism to involve non-muscle myosin IIA (NMIIA) polarization towards the soft-matrix-side but may not require differential actin flow up- or down-stiffness gradient.
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data showing NMIIA localization (Figure 3) and knockdown experiments.

claim: Amoeboid durotaxis may not require differential actin flow up- or down-stiffness gradient.
source: We further delineate the underlying mechanism to involve non-muscle myosin IIA (NMIIA) polarization towards the soft-matrix-side but may not require differential actin flow up- or down-stiffness gradient.
evidence: Supported by actin flow measurements showing no difference between soft and stiff sides (Figure 2B).

claim: Amoeboid durotaxis is evolutionarily conserved, as demonstrated in Dictyostelium.
source: Using the protista Dictyostelium, we demonstrate the evolutionary conservation of amoeboid durotaxis.
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing Dictyostelium exhibits durotaxis (Figure 4).

claim: An active gel model capable of mechanosensing theoretically captures amoeboid durotaxis phenomena.
source: Finally, these experimental phenomena are theoretically captured by an active gel model capable of mechanosensing.
evidence: Supported by computational simulations shown in Figures 5 and 6.

claim: The stiffness gradient of polyacrylamide gels was 20.77 kPa/mm.
source: Typically, cells were sandwiched between two polyacrylamide (PA) gels (Figure 1A iv) with stiffness gradient (20.77 kPa/mm, Figure 1—figure supplement 1A) or uniform stiffness (Rong et al., 2021).
evidence: Measured by atomic force microscopy as shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claim: T cells undergo typical amoeboid migration with relatively high speed (mean velocity of 16.21 μm/min).
source: As reported previously (Shannon et al., 2019), we observed that T cells underwent typical amoeboid migration with relatively high speed (the mean velocity was 16.21 μm/min) (Figure 1B and E, Videos 1 and 2), distinguished from mesenchymal migration which is usually below 1 μm/min (Bear and Haugh, 2014).
evidence: Supported by velocity measurements from live cell imaging data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: T cells lack stable focal adhesions, as evidenced by diffused paxillin signals.
source: When we stained these T cells for focal adhesion marker paxillin (Wang et al., 2021), we detected diffused signals by ultrastructure expansion microscopy (U-ExM) (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B), distinguished from the plaque-like structure in mesenchymal cells such as the MDA-MB-231 (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence imaging shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B and 1C.

claim: T cells on uniform gel showed random motility with FMI around zero.
source: FMI for cells on the uniform gel was around zero (indicating random motility) (Figure 1E), while it displayed a positive value for cells on the stiffness gradient gel and significantly exceeded that of cells on the uniform gel (Figure 1E).
evidence: Supported by FMI measurements shown in Figure 1E.

claim: T cells on stiffness gradient gel displayed positive FMI values significantly exceeding those on uniform gel.
source: FMI for cells on the uniform gel was around zero (indicating random motility) (Figure 1E), while it displayed a positive value for cells on the stiffness gradient gel and significantly exceeded that of cells on the uniform gel (Figure 1E).
evidence: Supported by FMI measurements shown in Figure 1E with statistical significance (p<0.0001).

claim: Stiffness gradient did not enhance T cell motility but increased forward migratory tendency.
source: Besides, no obvious difference in velocity was detected when comparing T cells moving on uniform vs gradient gel (Figure 1E), indicating that stiffness gradient did not enhance motility but rather increased forward migratory tendency.
evidence: Supported by velocity measurements showing no significant difference between conditions (Figure 1E).

claim: Neutrophils display durotactic behavior on gradient gels.
source: In line with our observations with T cells, neutrophils displayed random gliding on the uniform gel while appeared to durotax on the gradient gel, as revealed by the FMI and angular displacement analysis (Figure 1F–I, Video 3).
evidence: Supported by FMI and angular displacement data shown in Figure 1F-I.

claim: Some neutrophils exhibit highly persistent migration while others frequently change directions but show stiff-end biased migration overall.
source: When analyzing live cell trajectories, we found that some cells indeed exhibited highly persistent migration (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D, Track 1, 7, 9, 14, Video 4). However, we also detected cells that frequently changed directions but showed stiff-end biased migration on the whole (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D, Track 4, 5, 8, 10, Video 4).
evidence: Supported by trajectory analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1D and Video 4.

claim: Neutrophils on stiffness gradient gel did not elevate their persistence compared to those on uniform gel.
source: Analysis of the bulk cell population revealed that neutrophils on stiffness gradient gel did not elevate their persistence compared to those on the uniform gel (Figure 1I).
evidence: Supported by persistence measurements shown in Figure 1I.

claim: Differentiated HL-60 (dHL-60) cells employ amoeboid migration.
source: In agreement with previous reports, we detected that HL-60 employs amoeboid migration when differentiated into neutrophil-like cells (dHL-60) (Collins et al., 1978; Figure 1J, Figure 1—figure supplement 3, Video 5).
evidence: Supported by imaging data (Figure 1J, Figure 1—figure supplement 3) and previous literature (Collins et al., 1978).

claim: dHL-60 cells migrate randomly on uniform gel and towards the stiff end on gradient gel under confinement.
source: dHL-60 cells migrated randomly on the uniform gel while moving towards the stiff end on gradient gel (Figure 1J–M, Video 5) under confinement.
evidence: Supported by trajectory and FMI data shown in Figure 1J-M.

claim: Actin flow velocity in dHL-60 cells drops sharply when cells are plated on stiffer substrate (160 kPa) compared to soft gel (4 kPa).
source: Retrograde flow analysis (Mendoza et al., 2012) revealed that actin flow velocity dropped sharply when cells were plated on the stiffer substrate (160 kPa) compared to the soft gel (4 kPa) (Figure 2A, Videos 6 and 7).
evidence: Supported by quantitative fluorescent speckle microscopy data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: A descending trend of actin flow speed was detected with increasing substrate stiffness.
source: Moreover, a descending trend of actin flow speed was detected with increasing substrate stiffness (Figure 2A, Videos 6–10), suggesting that actin flow in amoeboid cells can indeed respond to stiffness.
evidence: Supported by actin flow measurements across different stiffness conditions shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Actin flow in amoeboid cells can respond to substrate stiffness.
source: Moreover, a descending trend of actin flow speed was detected with increasing substrate stiffness (Figure 2A, Videos 6–10), suggesting that actin flow in amoeboid cells can indeed respond to stiffness.
evidence: Inferred from the observed correlation between actin flow speed and substrate stiffness.

claim: Actin flow in up-gradient and down-gradient regions of cells on gradient gel appeared similar in speed.
source: However, against our hypothesis, actin flow in these two regions appeared similar in speed (Figure 2B, Video 11).
evidence: Supported by actin flow measurements comparing soft and stiff sides shown in Figure 2B.

claim: CK-666 treatment significantly decreased actin flow speed in T cells.
source: Upon CK-666 treatment, we observed a significant decrease in actin flow speed (Figure 2C) while the durotactic behavior was not impacted (Figure 2D), indicating that actin flow may not play a crucial role in amoeboid durotaxis.
evidence: Supported by actin flow measurements after CK-666 treatment shown in Figure 2C.

claim: CK-666 treatment did not impact durotactic behavior of T cells.
source: Upon CK-666 treatment, we observed a significant decrease in actin flow speed (Figure 2C) while the durotactic behavior was not impacted (Figure 2D), indicating that actin flow may not play a crucial role in amoeboid durotaxis.
evidence: Supported by FMI measurements showing no significant difference after CK-666 treatment (Figure 2D).

claim: Actin flow may not play a crucial role in amoeboid durotaxis.
source: Upon CK-666 treatment, we observed a significant decrease in actin flow speed (Figure 2C) while the durotactic behavior was not impacted (Figure 2D), indicating that actin flow may not play a crucial role in amoeboid durotaxis.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that reducing actin flow speed did not affect durotaxis.

claim: Microtubule perturbation (Nocodazole or Taxol) did not alter durotactic FMI in T cells.
source: However, no obvious alterations in durotactic FMI were detected under treatments of either the microtubule polymerization inhibitor Nocodazole or the depolymerization inhibitor Taxol (Figure 2E, Figure 2—figure supplement 1, Videos 12 and 13; Rong et al., 2021; Tabdanov et al., 2021), indicating that similar influence of the microtubule network on mesenchymal cells may not apply to amoeboid durotaxis.
evidence: Supported by FMI measurements after drug treatments shown in Figure 2E.

claim: Microtubule network influence on mesenchymal cells may not apply to amoeboid durotaxis.
source: However, no obvious alterations in durotactic FMI were detected under treatments of either the microtubule polymerization inhibitor Nocodazole or the depolymerization inhibitor Taxol (Figure 2E, Figure 2—figure supplement 1, Videos 12 and 13; Rong et al., 2021; Tabdanov et al., 2021), indicating that similar influence of the microtubule network on mesenchymal cells may not apply to amoeboid durotaxis.
evidence: Inferred from the lack of effect of microtubule perturbation on amoeboid durotaxis.

claim: Blebbistatin treatment drastically reduced durotactic FMI of T cells and neutrophils towards zero.
source: Interestingly, treating T cells or neutrophils with the NMII inhibitor blebbistatin to disrupt cell contraction drastically reduced durotactic FMI towards zero (Figure 2F and G, Video 14).
evidence: Supported by FMI measurements after blebbistatin treatment shown in Figure 2F and G.

claim: Rho activator II treatment elevated the FMI of durotactic T cells and neutrophils.
source: In contrast, Rho activator II, which can enhance myosin contractility, elevated the FMI of durotactic T cells and neutrophils (Figure 2F and G), supporting the notion that NMII activation may play an important role in amoeboid durotaxis.
evidence: Supported by FMI measurements after Rho activator II treatment shown in Figure 2F and G.

claim: NMII activation may play an important role in amoeboid durotaxis.
source: In contrast, Rho activator II, which can enhance myosin contractility, elevated the FMI of durotactic T cells and neutrophils (Figure 2F and G), supporting the notion that NMII activation may play an important role in amoeboid durotaxis.
evidence: Inferred from the effects of NMII inhibition and activation on durotaxis.

claim: Loss of NMIIA rather than NMIIB abolished dHL-60 durotaxis.
source: Interestingly, cell trajectories on gradient gel revealed that loss of NMIIA rather than NMIIB abolished dHL-60 durotaxis (Figure 3B–E, Video 15), which was not in accordance with what has been reported in mesenchymal cells (Raab et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by FMI measurements in NMIIA and NMIIB knockdown cells shown in Figure 3B-E.

claim: NMIIB protein level in NMIIAKD cells doubled while there was no compensatory upregulation of NMIIA in NMIIBKD cells.
source: The results showed that NMIIB protein level in NMIIAKD cells doubled while there was no compensatory upregulation of NMIIA in NMIIBKD cells (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B, C), further suggesting NMIIA rather than NMIIB is responsible for amoeboid durotaxis since in NMIIAKD cells, compensatory upregulation of NMIIB did not rescue the durotaxis-deficient phenotype.
evidence: Supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1B and C.

claim: NMIIA rather than NMIIB is responsible for amoeboid durotaxis.
source: The results showed that NMIIB protein level in NMIIAKD cells doubled while there was no compensatory upregulation of NMIIA in NMIIBKD cells (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B, C), further suggesting NMIIA rather than NMIIB is responsible for amoeboid durotaxis since in NMIIAKD cells, compensatory upregulation of NMIIB did not rescue the durotaxis-deficient phenotype.
evidence: Inferred from knockdown experiments showing NMIIA is required but NMIIB is not.

claim: NMIIA was concentrated at the down-gradient side of dHL-60 cells, regardless of the front-rear axis of the cell.
source: Strikingly, NMIIA was concentrated at the down-gradient side of dHL-60 cells, regardless of the front-rear axis of the cell (Figure 3F and G).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence imaging and quantification shown in Figure 3F and G.

claim: NMIIB showed much less correlation with the stiffness gradient compared to NMIIA.
source: On the contrary, NMIIB showed much less correlation with the stiffness gradient (Figure 3G), consistent with it playing a minor role in the establishment of durotactic direction.
evidence: Supported by fluorescence intensity ratio measurements shown in Figure 3G.

claim: Similar distribution of NMIIA (soft-end polarized) was observed in T cells and neutrophils on gradient gel.
source: Similar distribution of NMIIA was also seen in T cells and neutrophils on gradient gel (Figure 3H, Figure 3—figure supplement 1D, E).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence imaging shown in Figure 3H and Figure 3—figure supplement 1D, E.

claim: GFP-NMIIA signal stayed concentrated at the soft side during cell re-polarization events.
source: We captured events when cells turned to align with the stiffness gradient and in these cases, the GFP-NMIIA signal stayed concentrated at the soft side, preceding re-polarization of the cell to form a new front-rear axis (Figure 3—figure supplement 2A, Video 16).
evidence: Supported by live cell imaging of GFP-NMIIA shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2A and Video 16.

claim: Dictyostelium exhibited stiff-side directed motility when seeded on gradient gel.
source: Agreeing with our previous findings with T cells and neutrophils, Dictyostelium also displayed stiff-side directed motility when seeded on the gradient gel (Figure 4A–D, Video 17).
evidence: Supported by trajectory and FMI analysis shown in Figure 4A-D.

claim: Blebbistatin application drastically dropped the durotactic FMI of Dictyostelium to around zero.
source: Blebbistatin application drastically dropped the durotactic FMI to around zero (Figure 4E), while Rho activator II treatment significantly elevated this value (Figure 4E).
evidence: Supported by FMI measurements after blebbistatin treatment shown in Figure 4E.

claim: Rho activator II treatment significantly elevated the durotactic FMI of Dictyostelium.
source: Blebbistatin application drastically dropped the durotactic FMI to around zero (Figure 4E), while Rho activator II treatment significantly elevated this value (Figure 4E).
evidence: Supported by FMI measurements after Rho activator II treatment shown in Figure 4E.

claim: Microtubule perturbation did not hamper the directionality of Dictyostelium durotaxis.
source: Moreover, in line with what we discovered in T cells, microtubule perturbation did not hamper the directionality of Dictyostelium durotaxis (Figure 4F).
evidence: Supported by FMI measurements after microtubule perturbation shown in Figure 4F.

claim: The molecular mechanism underlying amoeboid durotaxis is largely conserved in Dictyostelium.
source: These results suggest that the molecular mechanism underlying amoeboid durotaxis is largely conserved in Dictyostelium.
evidence: Inferred from similar responses to blebbistatin, Rho activator, and microtubule perturbation in Dictyostelium as in mammalian cells.

claim: The active gel model predicts that cells initially placed on softer regions of gradient substrates exhibit stronger durotaxis.
source: In addition, the model predicts that cells initially placed on softer regions of gradient substrates exhibit stronger durotaxis (Figure 6C–E).
evidence: Supported by computational simulations shown in Figure 6C-E.

claim: Cells on the soft region of gradient gel showed highest FMI, while cells in the stiff region displayed more random motility.
source: FMI of cells on the soft region topped, while cells in the stiff region displayed more random motility (Figure 6G).
evidence: Supported by experimental FMI measurements across different regions shown in Figure 6G.

claim: Cell velocity and persistence showed no difference among soft, middle, and stiff regions of gradient gel.
source: Cell velocity and persistence showed no difference among these regions (Figure 6H, I).
evidence: Supported by velocity and persistence measurements shown in Figure 6H and I.

claim: The proposed active gel model successfully recapitulates amoeboid durotaxis found in experiments.
source: The proposed model successfully recapitulates amoeboid durotaxis found in our experiments (Figure 5C–E).
evidence: Supported by comparison of model predictions with experimental observations shown in Figure 5.

claim: Asymmetric distribution of NMIIA is observed in simulations, where NMIIA displays high concentration at the rear of the cell.
source: In addition, asymmetric distribution of NMIIA is observed in our simulation, where NMIIA displays a high concentration at the rear of the cell (Figure 5E), consistent with our experiments (Figure 3F).
evidence: Supported by computational simulations shown in Figure 5E and comparison with experimental data in Figure 3F.

claim: Durotaxis based on focal adhesion-dependent mechanosensing has been well studied for decades.
source: Durotaxis based on focal adhesion-dependent mechanosensing has been well studied for decades.
evidence: This is a statement about the state of the field, supported by general scientific knowledge.

claim: Cell migration is essential to myriads of physiological and pathological processes including cancer dissemination.
source: Cell migration is essential to myriads of physiological and pathological processes including cancer dissemination (Trepat et al., 2012).
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge supported by citation.

claim: The ability of cells to sense and navigate along higher substrate stiffness has been coined as 'durotaxis' in the early 2000s.
source: The ability of cells to sense and navigate along higher substrate stiffness has been coined as 'durotaxis' in the early 2000s (Lo et al., 2000) with important pathophysiological implications (Espina et al., 2022).
evidence: This is a historical statement about terminology supported by citations.

claim: Immune cells mainly undergo rapid single-cell crawling referred to as 'amoeboid' migration, without the formation of stable focal adhesions but can achieve migration ten times faster than mesenchymal migration.
source: In contrast to mesenchymal migration adopted by some tumor cells, immune cells mainly undergo rapid single-cell crawling referred to as 'amoeboid' migration, without the formation of stable focal adhesions but can achieve migration ten times faster (Shannon et al., 2019).
evidence: This is established knowledge about immune cell migration supported by citation.

claim: Modeling on amoeboid migration suggested that myosin contractility may play an important role when mechanical anchoring is less evident.
source: Modeling on amoeboid migration suggested that myosin contractility may play an important role when mechanical anchoring is less evident (Hawkins et al., 2011).
evidence: This is a statement about previous modeling work supported by citation.

claim: Actomyosin was described as an active gel whose polarity dictates the alignment of actin fibers.
source: In this model, actomyosin was described as an active gel whose polarity dictates the alignment of actin fibers (Hawkins et al., 2011).
evidence: This describes a previous modeling approach supported by citation.

claim: In silico simulation suggested that actomyosin contractility can lead to collective internal flows of actin, which, in turn, propels the cell body forward.
source: Moreover, in silico simulation suggested that actomyosin contractility can lead to collective internal flows of actin, which, in turn, propels the cell body forward (Tjhung et al., 2012).
evidence: This describes previous simulation results supported by citation.

claim: During development and immune surveillance, chemotactic cues have been reported to globally prescribe the migratory direction and destination of immune cells.
source: During development and immune surveillance, chemotactic cues have been reported to globally prescribe the migratory direction and destination of immune cells (Carles and Pittet, 2010).
evidence: This is established knowledge about immune cell guidance supported by citation.

claim: Previous studies have shown that inflamed, stiffened endothelial cells could induce more neutrophil transmigration.
source: Previous studies have shown that inflamed, stiffened endothelial cells could induce more neutrophil transmigration (Stroka and Aranda-Espinoza, 2011), and that once adhered to the endothelium, transmigrating neutrophils may exert durotactic sensing to search for stiffer sites (Schaefer and Hordijk, 2015).
evidence: This describes previous research findings supported by citations.

claim: Lymphocytes such as CD4+ Naïve T cells increased spreading area when plated on stiffer substrates.
source: In addition, lymphocytes such as CD4+ Naïve T cells increased spreading area when plated on stiffer substrates (Saitakis et al., 2017), indicative of the capacity to sense external mechanical signal.
evidence: This describes previous research findings supported by citation.

claim: Amoeboid cells, albeit without strong adhesions, are able to sense and respond to environmental stiffness.
source: The above evidence argue that amoeboid cells, albeit without strong adhesions, are able to sense and respond to environmental stiffness.
evidence: This is inferred from the cited evidence about neutrophil and T cell mechanosensing.

claim: NMIIB is more sensitive to stiffness gradient than NMIIA in mesenchymal stem cells.
source: It has been documented that NMIIB is more sensitive to stiffness gradient than NMIIA in mesenchymal stem cells (Raab et al., 2012).
evidence: This describes previous research findings supported by citation.

claim: When mesenchymal cells crawl on rigid glass, NMIIB is enriched at the cell rear.
source: Previous studies showed that when mesenchymal cells crawl on rigid glass, NMIIB is enriched at the cell rear (Sandquist et al., 2006), whereas NMIIA appears uniformly distributed (Raab et al., 2012).
evidence: This describes previous research findings supported by citations.

claim: NMIIA appears uniformly distributed in mesenchymal cells crawling on rigid glass.
source: Previous studies showed that when mesenchymal cells crawl on rigid glass, NMIIB is enriched at the cell rear (Sandquist et al., 2006), whereas NMIIA appears uniformly distributed (Raab et al., 2012).
evidence: This describes previous research findings supported by citation.

claim: Localizing NMIIA to the cell rear is required to set cell polarity.
source: Previous studies suggested that localizing NMIIA to the cell rear is required to set cell polarity (Raab et al., 2012; Jacobelli et al., 2004).
evidence: This describes previous research findings supported by citations.

claim: Substrate rigidity influences differentiation, gene expression, cell migration, morphology, and cytokine secretion in T cells.
source: Substrate rigidity influences differentiation (O'Connor et al., 2012), gene expression, cell migration, morphology, and cytokine secretion (Saitakis et al., 2017) in T cells.
evidence: This describes previous research findings supported by citations.

claim: Cytotoxic T lymphocytes (CTL) have been shown to enhance killing response when encountering stiffer target cells.
source: Interestingly, cytotoxic T lymphocytes (CTL) have been shown to enhance killing response when encountering stiffer target cells (Basu et al., 2016).
evidence: This describes previous research findings supported by citation.

claim: Fibrosis is characterized by tissue stiffening due to excessive extracellular matrix protein deposition and cross-linking.
source: Fibrosis is characterized by tissue stiffening due to excessive extracellular matrix protein deposition and cross-linking (Wells, 2013).
evidence: This is established knowledge about fibrosis supported by citation.

claim: Inorganic droplets can move directionally on surfaces with a stiffness gradient due to the intrinsic wettability.
source: Inorganic droplets can move directionally on surfaces with a stiffness gradient due to the intrinsic wettability (Bueno et al., 2018; Pallarès et al., 2023).
evidence: This describes previous research findings supported by citations.

claim: Droplets with smaller and wetting contact angles move towards the soft end, while those with larger and non-wetting contact angles can durotax.
source: Droplets with smaller and wetting contact angles move towards the soft end, while those with larger and non-wetting contact angles can durotax (Bueno et al., 2018).
evidence: This describes previous research findings supported by citation.

claim: dHL-60 cells have non-wetting contact angles (greater than 90 degrees) on both stiffer and softer sides of gradient gel.
source: We also measured the contact angles of dHL-60 cells at both the stiffer and softer sides on gradient gel and observed non-wetting contact angles (greater than 90 degrees) on both sides (Figure 3—figure supplement 2C) albeit the angles on the softer side are larger (Figure 3—figure supplement 2D).
evidence: Supported by contact angle measurements shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2C and D.

claim: The contact angles on the softer side of dHL-60 cells are larger than on the stiffer side.
source: We also measured the contact angles of dHL-60 cells at both the stiffer and softer sides on gradient gel and observed non-wetting contact angles (greater than 90 degrees) on both sides (Figure 3—figure supplement 2C) albeit the angles on the softer side are larger (Figure 3—figure supplement 2D).
evidence: Supported by contact angle measurements shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2D.

claim: The smaller, non-wetting contact angle on the stiffer side is likely to contribute to amoeboid durotaxis to a certain extent.
source: Hence, it can be postulated that the smaller, non-wetting contact angle on the stiffer side is also likely to contribute to amoeboid durotaxis to a certain extent.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the contact angle measurements and previous literature on droplet movement.

claim: The identification that rigidity-guided migration existed in low-adhesive, fast-moving amoeboid cells may provide new insights in focal adhesion-independent mechanosensing.
source: Together, the identification that rigidity-guided migration existed in low-adhesive, fast-moving amoeboid cells may provide new insights in focal adhesion-independent mechanosensing, and may shed new lights on immune surveillance and cancer metastasis.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about the implications of the findings.

claim: The findings may shed new lights on immune surveillance and cancer metastasis.
source: Together, the identification that rigidity-guided migration existed in low-adhesive, fast-moving amoeboid cells may provide new insights in focal adhesion-independent mechanosensing, and may shed new lights on immune surveillance and cancer metastasis.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about the implications of the findings.

claim: The down-gradient concentrated NMIIA may leverage the cell front towards the stiffer side, thus enabling efficient amoeboid durotaxis.
source: We then hypothesized that the down-gradient concentrated NMIIA may leverage the cell front towards the stiffer side, thus enabling efficient amoeboid durotaxis.
evidence: This is a hypothesis proposed by the authors based on their observations.

claim: Mst1 kinase is a key component of the Hippo pathway that could be regulated by substrate stiffness.
source: Mst1 kinase is a key component of the Hippo pathway that could be regulated by substrate stiffness.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the Hippo pathway.

claim: Mst1 directly regulates NMIIA dynamics to organize high and low-affinity LFA-1 to the anterior and posterior membrane during T cell migration.
source: It has been reported that Mst1 directly regulates NMIIA dynamics to organize high and low-affinity LFA-1 to the anterior and posterior membrane during T cell migration (Xu et al., 2014).
evidence: This describes previous research findings supported by citation.

claim: The mDia1-like formin A, IQGAP-related proteins, and actin-bundling protein cortexillin localize like NMII to the rear of polarized, migrating Dictyostelium cells.
source: The mDia1-like formin A, IQGAP-related proteins, and actin-bundling protein cortexillin localize like NMII to the rear of polarized, migrating Dictyostelium cells, promoting the formation of cortical actin in the rear and allowing efficient cell migration in 2D-confined environments (Ramalingam et al., 2015).
evidence: This describes previous research findings supported by citation.

claim: SMIFH2 treatment slightly decreased migration velocity but did not impact the durotactic behavior of T cells.
source: We have used formin inhibitor SMIFH2 in our durotaxis assay and found this treatment slightly decreased migration velocity but did not impact the durotactic behavior of T cells (Figure 3—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2B.

claim: Actin flow is generated by monomer assembly at the leading edge and myosin contraction at the cell rear, while is slowed down by traction stress between the cell bottom and the substrate.
source: Actin flow is generated by monomer assembly at the leading edge and myosin contraction at the cell rear, while is slowed down by traction stress between the cell bottom and the substrate (Gardel et al., 2008).
evidence: This is established knowledge about actin flow supported by citation.

claim: Strain energy from the halting of actin flow transduces into a protruding force to counteract membrane tension at the cell front.
source: Strain energy from the halting of actin flow then transduces into a protruding force to counteract membrane tension at the cell front (Hons et al., 2018; Lim et al., 2010).
evidence: This is established knowledge about actin flow mechanics supported by citations.

claim: The protrusion rate is inversely related to the actin retrograde flow.
source: Thus, the protrusion rate is inversely related to the actin retrograde flow (Jurado et al., 2005).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: Continuous cycles of protrusion support forward cell migration.
source: It has been suggested that continuous cycles of protrusion support forward cell migration (Yolland et al., 2019).
evidence: This describes previous research findings supported by citation.

claim: Classic molecular clutch model attributed both single and collective mesenchymal durotaxis to the differential adhesion strength on distinct substrate stiffness.
source: Classic molecular clutch model attributed both single and collective mesenchymal durotaxis to the differential adhesion strength on distinct substrate stiffness (Sunyer et al., 2016; Plotnikov et al., 2012; Bangasser et al., 2017).
evidence: This describes previous modeling work supported by citations.

claim: Enhanced traction strain energy on the stiffer matrix indicates the presence of increased motors and clutches.
source: Enhanced traction strain energy on the stiffer matrix (Bangasser et al., 2017; Shin et al., 2010) indicates the presence of increased motors and clutches, which may then slow down the actin flow at adhesion sites by friction (Bangasser et al., 2017).
evidence: This describes previous research findings and their interpretation, supported by citations.

claim: Actin flow is mechanosensitive – with low speed on stiff substrate and high speed on soft matrix.
source: In this sense, actin flow is mechanosensitive – with low speed on stiff substrate and high speed on soft matrix.
evidence: This is inferred from the molecular clutch model and previous research.

claim: Interaction between Lymphocyte Function-Associated Antigen 1 (LFA-1) and its ligand Intercellular Adhesion Molecule 1 (ICAM-1) has been reported to drive T cell movement by creating tangential friction between the actin cortex and the environment.
source: Interaction between Lymphocyte Function-Associated Antigen 1 (LFA-1) and its ligand Intercellular Adhesion Molecule 1 (ICAM-1) has been reported to drive T cell movement by creating tangential friction between the actin cortex and the environment (Hons et al., 2018).
evidence: This describes previous research findings supported by citation.

claim: T cells were allowed to migrate on the ICAM-1 coated surface in the experiments.
source: In this case, T cells were allowed to migrate on the ICAM-1 coated surface.
evidence: This describes the experimental setup used in the study.

claim: CK-666 is an Arp2/3 complex inhibitor that prevents branched actin formation.
source: To further explore the role of actin flow in durotaxis, we took advantage of CK-666, an Arp2/3 complex inhibitor that prevents branched actin formation, to decrease actin flow speed without changing NMII localization (Yang et al., 2012; Henson et al., 2015).
evidence: This is established knowledge about CK-666 supported by citations.

claim: CK-666 decreases actin flow speed without changing NMII localization.
source: To further explore the role of actin flow in durotaxis, we took advantage of CK-666, an Arp2/3 complex inhibitor that prevents branched actin formation, to decrease actin flow speed without changing NMII localization (Yang et al., 2012; Henson et al., 2015).
evidence: This describes previous research findings about CK-666 effects, supported by citations.

claim: Migrating amoeboid cells commonly form spherical protrusions called blebs at their leading edges, which facilitate cell locomotion.
source: Migrating amoeboid cells commonly form spherical protrusions called blebs at their leading edges, which facilitate cell locomotion (Schick and Raz, 2022).
evidence: This is established knowledge about amoeboid cell migration supported by citation.
